articleTitle: Doubly fed induction generator systems for wind turbines
abstract: THE AIM OF WIND TURBINE SYSTEMS DEVELOPMENT is to continuously increase output power. A few years ago, the rated output power of production-type units reached 200 kW. By 1999, the average output power of new installations climbed to 600 kW. The largest series production units today are specified to deliver 1.5-MW output power (Table 1). It is anticipated that in the near future, power rating of wind turbines will increase further, especially in offshore applications. For example, the prototype of a Nordex N80 with a rated power of 2.5 MW was installed in March 2000 near Aachen.

articleTitle: Distributed generation
abstract: THE DEREGULATION OF UTILITIES and the emerging power markets are creating renewed interest in operating generators in parallel with the utility system. Some of the more common reasons are □ utility perspective □ transmission capacity relief □ distribution capacity relief □ hedge against high market prices.

articleTitle: Realization of a smart electrolytic capacitor circuit
abstract: THANKS TO THEIR LARGE capacity and low price, electrolytic capacitors are often used for filtering and energy storage applications. The major disadvantage of these components is their low reliability. Software and electronic modules have been developed to compute the lifetime of electrolytic capacitors online [1]-[3], but these monitoring systems haves three main drawbacks: □ They are rather expensive. □ They depend on the static converter structure. □ They cannot predict the fault of one capacitor if several capacitors are in parallel.

articleTitle: Bearing fluting [motors]
abstract: WHEN UNEXPECTED BEARING LOSSES WERE QUESTIONED AT A PAPER MILL, work began at the mill that led to a long-term investigation to determine the causes and incidence of a type of bearing damage called “bearing fluting.” It was discovered that many paper machines have bearing fluting that has caused significant down time and increased maintenance costs. Additionally, bearing fluting was found to be associated with the use of ac or dc sectional variable-speed control. This problem is not new, but the understanding of its origin, magnitude, and treatment has improved over the past couple of years. A number of ways to control the problem were investigated. Our first encounter with bearing fluting, that we were aware of, occurred in 1988 on a kraft paper machine approximately one year after it was rebuilt. The rebuild included replacement of a line shaft with 26 dc drives and four ac drives. The first bearing problem appeared in a dryer-drive dc motor. Within three years, we had found and replaced fluted bearings in nearly all of the variable-speed ac motors and 24 of the 26 dc motors.

articleTitle: LED wireless
abstract: THE SUPERIORITY OF LIGHT-EMIT-ting diodes (LEDs) over incandescent lights, due to long life expectancy, high tolerance to humidity, low power consumption, and minimal heat generation, is well supported. LEDs are used in message display boards, signal devices, and many other means of illumination. One important characteristic of LEDs is that they are semiconductor devices capable of fast switching with the addition of appropriate electronics. That is, the visible light emitted by LEDs can be modulated and encoded with audio information for broadcasting. Therefore, in addition to their normal functions as indication and illumination devices, LEDs can be used as communication devices for transmitting and broadcasting audio and digital information. Hence, they can become part of wireless optical-communication systems. This article describes an information system for the broadcasting of audio and digital signals using visible LEDs.

articleTitle: Internet-based monitoring and controls for HVAC applications
abstract: SIGNIFICANT ADVANCES in Internet and computer technology have made it possible to develop an Internet-based control, monitoring, and operation scheduling system for heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems. The proposed system architecture includes such features as control, measurement, networking, and reporting. This article addresses issues in architecture selection, electronics, embedded processors and software, and Internet technologies. This article also proposes an Internet-based HVAC system architecture that combines Web technology, networking, and functions of direct digital control. The proposed system also includes technologies needed for supporting real-time digital thermostat control, data gathering, remote access and occupancy control, light sensing control, and views of the history of HVAC utilization. This system enables users to make cost-effective energy decisions and quickly identify trouble spots of HVAC systems to minimize system down time.

articleTitle: Bright idea, radio-frequency light sources
abstract: THE IDEA OF RADIO FREQUENCY (RF) LIGHTING, as well as the first RF lamp patent, appeared long before the first fluorescent and high-pressure lamps came onto the market. It took over a century for the first commercial RF lamp to appear, introducing a new era in the production of light. Recent progress in semiconductor power switching electronics, along with a more thorough understanding of fundamental processes in RF plasmas, have resulted in commercially viable RF light sources.

articleTitle: Ride-through for critical loads. Exploring a low-cost approach to maintaining continuous connections between buildings and/or industrial systems
abstract: ALTHOUGH NUMEROUS EFFORTS have recently been put in place to increase the reliability and quality of existing electric systerns, it seems like power quality still has not reached the desired levels to be consistent with the high degree of automatization and sophistication that modern electronic equipment have. In this matter, voltage sags are the most prevalent disturbances in electric power systems; a recent survey attributes them to 92% of all disturbances [1], Most electronic loads are sensitive to voltage variations, which can lower their performance or even shut down the process that they control. With the increased use of large converter-based loads in industry, computers for office automation, and other sensitive electronic circuitry, electric power quality has become an important issue. Special attention has focused on critical loads, such as medical centers [2], automobile manufacturing plants [3], the semiconductor industry [4], broadcasting facilities, and commercial buildings [5]. In all of these cases, numerous electronic loads are sensitive to voltage sags and disturbances. Although the exact cost of poor power quality cannot be known with certainty, it is estimated that voltage sag disturbances cost millions of dollars every year in the United States [4]-[7].

articleTitle: Power modules for appliance motor control
abstract: THE USE OF INVERTERS IN APPLIANCE APPLICATIONS is increasing rapidly. Although the idea of inverterized appliances is new for the United States, it is not in other parts of the world. The charts in Fig. 1 show the appliance market for air conditioners, refrigerators, washing machines, and vacuums in North America and Japan. In Japan, 37% of the appliance market is already inverterized, while less than 1% of the U.S. market is. There is a great deal of potential for inverterized appliances in the United States.

articleTitle: Automotive HID headlamps producing compact electronic ballasts using power ICs
abstract: INCANDESCENT HALOGEN LAMPS have been the standard for automotive headlamps; however, metal halide high-intensity discharge (HID) lamps have slowly begun to be commercially used since the mid-1990s. The lighting system of the metal halide HID headlamp makes a great contribution to energy savings, longer lamp life and better visibility in traffic zones compared with halogen lamps. (Lamp life is lengthened because it prevents the loss of sodium metal as plus ions through the quartz of the lamp bulb.) This article describes power ICs consisting of full bridge inverters and their drivers in detail.

articleTitle: Evaluation of maximum rotor temperatures in TEFC inverter-fed motors
abstract: When installing an induction motor in a Class I, Division 2 hazardous (classified) area, it is H Y in the interest of both the user and the manufacturer to insure that the installed motor will not become a source of ignition of flammable gases or vapors in the classified area. Article 501 of the National Electrical Code, NFPA 70, contains regulations governing such motor installations [1]. Article 501-8(b) allows the use of explosion-proof motors or “open or nonexplosion-proof enclosed motors, such as squirrel-cage induction motors without brushes, switching mechanisms, or similar arc-producing devices….” Fine Print Note No. 1, which follows Article 501-8(b), then instructs the reader that “It is important to consider the temperature of internal and external surfaces that may be exposed to the flammable atmosphere.”

articleTitle: TVSS designs
abstract: Transient-voltage surge SUPPRESSION (TVSS) is a very necessary ingredient for most electronic and computer devices that are exposed to telecommunications or power lines. Nevertheless, effective application, design, and manufacturing still tends to be more art than science. We have conducted over 100 tests of various commercial devices. As a part of the project, the design of effective devices was pursued. Fortunately, the best devices are actually quite inexpensive.

articleTitle: Charles LeGeyt Fortescue and the method of symmetrical components
abstract: In 1918, the Transactions of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers (AIEE) included a classic paper by Charles LeGeyt Fortescue entitled “Method of Symmetrical Co-Ordinates Applied to the Solution of Polyphase Networks” (Fig. 1). The author was an engineer with the Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Company in Pittsburgh, PA, where he spent his entire professional career. The method of analysis that was the theme of his paper soon became known as the method of symmetrical components, and it greatly facilitated the analysis of unbalanced polyphase systems by converting problems into equivalent symmetrical systems. Fortescue was elected a Fellow of the AIEE in 1921 and received the Elliot Cresson Medal of the Franklin Institute in recognition of the importance of his contribution to symmetrical component theory and application. He also made important contributions to investigations related to the protection of transmission lines from lightning, the design of high-voltage insulators and transformers, and the development of the ac calculating board.

articleTitle: Dim the lights. Problems with lamp current control using a PWM signal
abstract: IT IS THE STATE OF THE ART to drive a fluorescent lamp with a ballast that mainly consists of a high-frequency generator. High frequency, in this context, means a frequency that is substantially higher than the mains frequency. Most ballasts on the market are working at an operating frequency of about 50 kHz. It is common to realize the high-frequency generator with a half-bridge inverter. This inverter has an output waveform with a rectangular shape, and the operating frequency F<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0</inf> is equal to the frequency of the oscillation of the half-bridge. The fluorescent lamp is connected to the output of the inverter via a matching network.

articleTitle: A touch of gray [power contacts, silver corrosion, whiskers growth]
abstract: SULFUR-RICH ENVIRONMENTS, such as those found in the paper and pulp industry, create a special problem with the silver plating in switchgear and motor control centers (MCCs). Silver plating is used throughout switchgear because of its superior conductivity and longevity. Silver is very sensitive to the presence of hydrogen sulfide (H<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>S), which forms silver sulfide (Ag<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>S), even at a very low concentration of corrosive gas. Nonuniform growth occurs in forms of “clumps,” “dendrites,” “nodules,” and “whiskers” [1]. The decomposition of the contact surfaces leads to an increase of the contact resistance, hence, to a rise in temperature, and eventually to possible failure. This article analyzes the major factors initiating and accelerating the growth of the whiskers on silver plating in electrical apparatus.

articleTitle: An artistic design system for industrial product image retrieval
abstract: THIS ARTICLE DESCRIBES A NEW TYPE of expert system that retrieves images of existing industrial products using a sketched image drawn by a designer on the basis of artistic industry designs. In this method, sketched images are applied to an artistic design system for industrial products so that designers can conceive actual images of completed products and their applications, referring to practical products which have been realized before. Image retrieval is carried our by comparing the sketched image to the images of allied products. In a series of studies, the success rate was as high as 75–78%, thus confirming the applicability of this system. This concept is expected to be applied to the artistic design of industrial products. Examples are given for the following products: a vase, garments, and shoes.

articleTitle: Charles F. Scott: a pioneer in electrical power engineering
abstract: One hundred years ago (1902–1903), Charles F. Scott (Fig. 1) was President of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers (AIEE). Already well known to the power engineering community for his invention of the Scott transformer connection (Fig. 2) and his investigation of high voltage transmission, he undertook a number of significant initiatives during his tenure as AJEE president. These were intended to enhance the status of electrical engineers and to increase the outreach of the AJEE. His career pattern was somewhat unusual in that he devoted the second half of his professional career to electrical engineering education.

articleTitle: Westinghouse and the AC system-1884-1895
abstract: During the early 1880s, in the mind of George Westinghouse the key to economically delivering electric power over a wide area lay in successfully developing an ac system. High voltage would be generated at the source, then lowered as it was delivered to users at the proper voltage required by each type of user, whether industrial or domestic.

articleTitle: Full-digital control boards for IGBT full-bridge switching converters
abstract: On the field of thermonuclear fusion research, the need to implement coil systems supplied to perform local controls of magnetic fluxes or to generate rotating magnetic fields has grown in the past few years [1]. Tens of coils, each one able to produce up to tens of millitesla on a surface of hundreds of square centimeters, have to be independently fed by converters rated for powers of hundreds of kilowatts and bandwidth in the order of hundreds of hertz.

articleTitle: How effectively do materials shield against transient electric fields?
abstract: SHIELDING” BY MATERIALS IS THE REDUCTION IN AMPLITUDE of a signal observed near a source by the insertion of material between the source and the application or point of observation. The “signal” may be as an electric or magnetic field.

articleTitle: What's your color? [human-machine interface design]
abstract: TAKE A WALK IN ANY PLANT with recently designed and installed human-machine interfaces (HMIs) and you will likely see screens in use that are vastly better than those of even the recent past. As graphical operator interfaces become more prevalent in our working world, it becomes increasingly important to focus on factors necessary to design the best screens possible. Recent improvements are generally due to advances in three major areas: increased understanding of the human factors involved in human-machine interface, more effective operator interface design, and improved operator terminal design and manufacture.

articleTitle: Acceleration tests to determine salient pole synchronous motor inrush currents and torques
abstract: DETERMINING TORQUE AND CURRENT at locked rotor and various slips during the acceleration test on a synchronous machine is very tedious and time consuming. Induction and synchronous machines behave similarly during acceleration except that synchronous machine acceleration can include a pulsation torque. Because of the salient poles, conditions exist where the synchronous motor has minimum torque at quadrature axis and maximum torque at direct axis during locked rotor or stall. Since synchronous machines do not have large numbers of rotor bars in the amortisseur winding, like the induction motor has in the squirrel cage, their stall times tend to be shorter. Due to the shorter stall time and large starting torque, locked-rotor torque and current are generally determined from acceleration tests conducted at reduced voltage rather than by tests at stand-still. Data showing that saturation effects impact both torque and current are presented here. The data shows that the voltage index that has to be applied to the torque and current measured at reduced voltage varies with speed and can be obtained from a series of acceleration tests.

articleTitle: Integrating process and motor control
abstract: For new industrial facilities, the use of multifunction microprocessor-based protection relays is common practice for medium-voltage motors and various electrical protective relaying. Typically, these devices have digital communication capability, primarily used for programming the device or equipment monitoring.

articleTitle: Electrical heat tracing: international harmonization-now and in the future
abstract: Electrical heat tracing has become a major and more complicated utility subsystem in production plants, increasing the focus placed on its control, monitoring, and electrical supply systems. This is especially true when heat tracing is used for process control. Although the supply of electrical power is governed by local codes and practices, electrical heat tracing is governed by approvals and company practice. In recent years, the Zone System has been introduced in North America, and installations using this classification are starting to appear.

articleTitle: Static VAr compensators-a solution to the big motor/weak system problem?
abstract: STATIC VAR COMPENSATORS (SVCs) with reactive power capabilities of hundreds of both positive and negative MVAR have been used for years by utilities to control reactive power flow in transmission and distribution systems. Smaller systems have been applied to industrial applications, principally for varying load situations, such as mine hoists, rolling mills, and arc furnaces. In recent years, some SVCs have been used to stabilize the utility and plant voltages in electrically remote locations, such as pumping stations, where relatively large motors are a major portion of the load. As well as being practical ways of controlling voltages, they are also often faster to supply and install than other utility solutions, such as getting approvals and installing new or higher voltage lines. It was found that a 0- to 30-MVAR SVC could be purchased, installed, and started up in less than one year at less cost than any utility solutions that could achieve the same voltage stabilization SVCs use solid-state switching devices to control reactive and capacitive currents flowing from the SVC to the power system. The switching can usually be controlled on a cycle-by-cycle basis, with reactive current and system voltage being used to determine the magnitude and phasing of the correction.

articleTitle: Tolerance rings [motor-overload protection]
abstract: Designers are constantly FACING THE CHALLENGES of packing more and more functionality into ever-smaller spaces while improving power and performance. Mechanical overload protection for drive-train systems has long been desirable but, in the past, has required bulky and expensive slip-clutch mechanisms.

articleTitle: Electric heat tracing: using electronic controls to enhance performance and safety
abstract: TODAY'S ELECTRONIC CONTROL systems for electrical heat tracing, when used with PC-based software, greatly improve system performance and reliability. Improved reliability results in lower cost of operations, less risk to the environment, and provides an installation with a high level of safety.

articleTitle: Minimizing burn injury: electric-arc hazard assessment and personnel protection
abstract: A SIGNIFICANT NUMBER OF SECOND- AND THIRD-DEGREE BURN INJURIES result from the intense radiant and convective energy of an electric arc [1]. These injuries frequently occur without electrical contact with the burn victim. The most serious of these burn injuries involve ignition of the victim's clothing by arc exposure. In this case, the continued burning of conventional work clothing increases both the burn depth and the total body area suffering burn injury. The total area of body burn injury is the key survival factor for burn victims based on the 1991–1993 American Burn Association (ABA) study [2]. Flame-resistant (FR) clothing can significantly reduce burn injury resulting from electric-arc exposure by avoiding clothing ignition and creating a thermal barrier that reduces arc exposure energy. Consequently, over the past several years, there has been increased emphasis by standards organizations and government regulatory agencies on the use of FR clothing by workers who are exposed to the electric-arc hazards. This article focuses on □ defining the level of arc exposure required to ignite conventional work clothing □ presenting guidelines for selecting FR clothing systems □ quantifying arc exposure as a function of electric system parameters.

articleTitle: The effects of plasma on electrostatic powder coating systems
abstract: IN ELECTROSTATIC POWDER COATING using a frictional charger, a serious problem is the poor charging characteristics of powder paint. In order to overcome this problem, we have investigated a new system composed of a plasma generator and a frictional charger. The results obtained for two kinds of polyester powder paints showed that the plasma has a strong effect on the characteristics of frictional charging in powder paint; the frictional charge was more than five times as large as that without plasma effects.

articleTitle: Education: past and future
abstract: It is with mixed emotions that I write this column, because this will be my last communication with you as Chairperson of the Education Department. In 2003,1 will assume the role of IAS Secretary, and the Education Department will come under the leadership of Joe Sottile (jsottile@engr.uky.edu), who is with the University of Kentucky. Joe is committed to providing continued quality leadership to the Education Department as we move to capitalize on the numerous opportunities that have arisen in areas related to the education of our members.

articleTitle: The Faraday bicentennial
abstract: Throughout the 20th I century, the development and application of I electrical technology has impacted virtually every facet of civilization. In fact, the U.S. National Academy of Engineering selected electrification as the single most significant engineering achievement of the 20th century. Power generation and distribution, communication, mass transportation, agriculture and food production, and diagnostic medicine are examples of the domains that were transformed by electrification. Other significant engineering accomplishments of the past century, such as space travel and automobiles, were dependent on electrical technologies. Just by browsing through the publications of the other 35 IEEE societies, I am reminded of the tremendous range of electrical technologies that are so integral to our modern way of life.

articleTitle: Brushing up on your maintenance practices
abstract: THE SUCCESSFUL LONG-TERM OPERATION OF DC MOTORS AND GENERATORS, like the operation of any piece of industrial equipment, requires maintenance. Scheduled, periodic, visual inspections and the recording of this data are valuable information when reviewing that machines' performance. These written inspection reports will serve much better than the memory of the maintenance technician or supervisor when questioning the performance history of a certain piece of equipment. A generic inspection record format is included, along with guidelines to help make decisions on the health status of these motors. This article will expand on ten major items of concern for the successful long-term operation of dc machines.

articleTitle: Heat tracing technology for the 21st century
abstract: THE FUNDAMENTAL CONCEPTS of electric heat tracing seem quite simple on the surface. However, anyone who has been involved in an electric heat tracing “design and build” project realizes the fallacy of this notion: □ Pipes are not always surrounded by perfect insulation envelopes. □ The insulation envelope can often be interrupted by pipe supports and other appendages that result in heat sink effects. □ Pipes and vessels are not solid structures; rather, they contain or are surrounded by fluids that can be in natural motion due to density gradients resulting from heating. □ Pipes may be constructed of nonthermally conductive materials, such as plastics, which have significantly reduced heat transfer coefficients and reduced temperature use ranges.

articleTitle: New science-new language
abstract: This article on changing technology and language was excerpted from previously unpublished portions of an earlier article about David Prince, the main body of which was published in a previous issue of this magazine [1]. The original article was quite lengthy and edited to meet available space. This excerpt was set aside for later publication since it contains some interesting background on switchgear ratings. The original excerpt is expanded somewhat to promote the idea of historical value in tracking word origins.

articleTitle: Zinc coating control on steel wires
abstract: Galvanized steel wires are mainly produced in hot dip galvanizing lines (Fig, 1). A device at the zinc pot output controls the coating thickness since the sensor usually measures this coating after the cooling process. Several wires run in parallel through the same zinc pot at speeds around 1 m/s.

articleTitle: Process control using a fiber-optic unified cabling systems
abstract: IΝ AN IDEAL WORLD, communications cabling for process control would be simple—buy all the computer, instrumentation, and electrical equipment from a single vendor, and connect it all together using a single cabling standard. But real life is never that simple; rarely are the programmable logic controllers (PLC), distributed control systems (DCS), drives, motor controls, field instrumentation, and computers all purchased from the same vendor. Even when they are, the vendor will often have a number of different vintages or models of equipment that require different cabling systems. The result is that most factories are faced with installing and maintaining many different cable systems, often with very inefficient cable layouts.

articleTitle: Vegetable-oil-based dielectric coolants
abstract: Electrical transformer insulation SYSTEMS are evaluated based on economic, safety, and environmental standpoints using total life cycle analysis. Because of the inherent high efficiency of liquid-cooled transformer designs, new developments focus on improving the environmental and safety properties of fire resistant (less-flammable, high fire point) fluids. This article reports the latest findings on dielectric systems using natural ester (vegetable oil) fluids. Because esters naturally have lower oxidation resistance than mineral oils, a novel blend of base oils and additives were developed to overcome this potential handicap. Single- and three-phase prototype field installations using these new dielectric coolants are discussed.

articleTitle: The transformer [historical overview]
abstract: The technological revolution that has shaped civilization since the 1880s sprang from fundamental advances in communications, transportation, and electric power. The crowning achievements of inventors in communications and transportation—the telephone, television, automobile, and airplane—are, by now, familiar fixtures of everyday life. In contrast, the invention that ensured the ubiquity of electric power goes largely unrecognized by those whose lives are touched by it. It is a device that does not move, is almost totally silent, and is typically hidden in underground vaults or stowed behind screens.

articleTitle: Copper versus aluminum-which construction is best? [induction motor rotors]
abstract: MANY INDUCTION MOTORS IN SERVICE TODAY are running critical processes in which failure at any time can be very costly. Many times, these critical processes will not have a back up. As a result, a large portion of these processes will shut down until the motor is repaired and put back into service. Those aware of this situation will strive to purchase a motor that will maximize reliability. As a result of the strong push for maximum reliability, it is easy to over specify costly components not required for specific applications. These decisions will result in an unnecessarily high motor purchase price. To maximize reliability without overspending, large induction motors need to be properly matched to specific applications. With this consideration, the choice between various rotor constructions needs to be evaluated. It is generally assumed that copper bar rotors are the most reliable. In certain applications, this may be true; they can at times outperform aluminum rotors. But many times, the applications are such that there will not be any appreciable performance or reliability benefit from the use of copper bar rotors. It will be shown that the percentage motor cost increase can be very large on smaller machines but may not be as significant on larger machines.

articleTitle: High-current DC choppers in the metals industry
abstract: All major power semiconductor companies are now manufacturing larger power switching devices, such as insulated gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs). Produced in the hundreds of thousands and distributed all over the world, IGBTs have been used in volume for many years for power applications, such as motor drives, frequency converters, and high-voltage and heavy-current dc power supplies. These power converters are used in many industries, including aerospace, transportation, mining, electrochemical, petrochemical, steel, environmental, and military. IGBT switching has become the accepted technology of choice [1], Recently, the application of IGBT-switching technology has been accepted as a means of controlling dc currents in high-power rectifier systems (referred to in this article as a “chopper rectifiers”) in the metals industries (steel and nonferrous) for electro-winning, dc arc furnace, graphite resistive heating, and plasma torch (used in metal heating) applications. This technology is also well suited for boosting dc current in aluminum pot line cells from existing rectifiers.

articleTitle: Maximizing large drive availability
abstract: Drive-system availability is a function of both the reliability and repair time of the drive, motor, and associated equipment. This is true at the system level, as well as at the component and subcomponent level. To achieve high availability, the reliability of each component as well as the drive itself must be reviewed. Various design methods can be used to improve reliability, such as modeling, component de-rating and margins, component redundancy, component qualification testing, and system qualification testing.

articleTitle: How to specify power-quality-tolerant process equipment
abstract: WITH THE INTENSE DRIVE FOR PROFITS, industrial plants are concerned about any kind of production shutdown. At the same time, sophisticated electronics are being rapidly introduced into most production processes. These are often in the form of such power-quality-sensitive equipment as □ computers □ telecommunications □ electronic process controls □ robotics □ adjustable-speed drives (ASDs).

articleTitle: Electric deregulation
abstract: Restructuring of the ELECTRIC INDUSTRY HAS BEGUN. In recent years, a number of states have adopted some sort of restructuring legislation or other enabling regulation. As the industry prepares itself to embrace the restructured environment, changes to individual utilities are inevitable.

articleTitle: Replace, refurbish, or retain? Evaluating aging electrical systems and equipment
abstract: Many of our electrical facilities were constructed or experienced major expansions in the 1950s and 1960s. We are now having to deal with electrical switchgear and systems that are 40 to 50 years old. Depending upon the environment and application of the equipment, they may be at or near the end of their useful lives.

articleTitle: Motor bearing systems
abstract: Numerous bearing systems are USED IN THE ELECTRIC MOTOR INDUSTRY. These systems even vary for a given manufacturer based on the motor size, type, enclosure, speed, and application. This article focuses on anti-friction rolling-element, grease- or oil-lubricated bearings used in vertical and horizontal motors. Although common in large motors, the hydrodynamic sleeve- and plate-type bearings are beyond the scope of this article. The primary focus will be on industrial applications that use more traditional types of bearings, lubricating systems, and enclosures. It is acknowledged that there are other specialized bearings in operation and other types of machinery where the principles of the article may have application.

articleTitle: Picking up the pieces. Utilizing disaster recovery project management to improve readiness and response time
abstract: AS IT CROSSED THE ATLANTIC OCEAN, Tropical Storm Georges grew and on 17 September 1998 became a full-fledged hurricane that would build to a Category 4 storm at its strongest. Hurricane Georges crossed the Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico, wreaking destruction on the U.S. Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic, Haiti, Cuba, and the Florida Keys, before finally hitting the U.S. Gulf Coast. Georges was responsible for approximately 500 deaths and over US$5 billion in damages. Fig. 1 shows the path of the destructive hurricane. On 28 September 1998, the hurricane hit land at Biloxi, Mississippi, USA, as a Category 2 storm with 105-mph sustained winds with gusts measured at up to 175 mph. There, the storm stalled for over 17 hours, pounding the area with its 12-foot storm surge, while dumping 16.68 in of rain [1], Fig. 2 gives an indication of the size of the hurricane and the area affected as Georges stalled upon striking land.

articleTitle: VF drives as final control elements in the petroleum industry
abstract: THE USE OF VARIABLE-FREQUENCY (VF) DRIVES (or adjustable-frequency drives) on electric motors driving centrifugal pumps can offer many advantages over using control valves when you need to control fluid flow. Some of the advantages include energy savings, efficiency, power factor, installation, specification, ability to control, maintenance, fugitive emissions, and reduced wear on the bearings and seals of the pumps.

articleTitle: Key learnings from the IAS Electrical Safety Workshops
abstract: In 1990, THE U.S. OCCUPATIONAL SAFETY AND HEALTH ADMINISTRATION issued the first of several regulations specifically aimed at reducing occupational injuries from electrical hazards in the workplace. The following year, the Petroleum and Chemical Industry Committee (PCIC) of the IEEE Industry Applications Society organized a Safety Subcommittee to address matters of electrical safety as related to the petrochemical industry. In developing its charter, the Safety Subcommittee, focused its efforts on organizing a technical papers session at the annual PCIC technical conference and complementing this with a separate annual forum or workshop for people to meet and exchange ideas for preventing workplace injuries from electrical hazards. The first workshop was held in March 1992 in Dallas, Texas, with 37 participants. The workshop goal was to accelerate the dispersion of understanding and knowledge of ongoing improvements in the practical application of codes, standards, and technology that reduce the risk of electrical injuries. Workshops have been held annually in North America since 1995. The Maintenance, Operation, and Safety Subcommittee of the IAS Industrial and Commercial Power Systems Department (in 1998) and the Pulp and Paper Industry Committee (in 2001) joined the PCIC Safety Subcommittee in organizing the subsequent workshops held in North America. Also in 1998, the Chair of IEEE/IAS Region 10 approached the PCIC Safety Subcommittee with a proposal to support a similar workshop in India. The workshop was held in Madras, India, in September 1998 with 43 participants. Based on its success, workshops were held in Delhi (2000) and Bombay (2002). The growth and expansion (Table 1) is an indicator of the value of this type of forum.

articleTitle: IEEE 1242: Guide for Specifying and Selecting Cable for Petrochemical Plants
abstract: THE PURPOSE OF THIS ARTICLE is to provide an overview of IEEE 12421999, Guide for Specifying and Selecting Power, Control, and Special Purpose Cable for Petroleum and Chemical Plants. This standard addresses wire and cable design, materials, testing, and installation, along with illustrations of typical constructions and application criteria. An extensive cross-referenced list of standards and technical papers, as they apply to the wire and cable industry, is included in the appendix of the standard.

articleTitle: A stitch in time...continuous supervision versus preventative maintenance-a new concept for petrochemical plants
abstract: CONTINUOUS SUPERVISION is a concept of preventative maintenance (PM) practices used in the German Chemical industry. It has recently been accepted inclusion into the IEC 60079-17 standard. It is a process where periodic checks are mandated on explosion protected equipment by skilled personnel. The level of scrutiny of these checks are determined by an “executive technician” or engineering manager.

articleTitle: Look before you leap! Practical tips for medium-voltage equipment check out
abstract: OVER THE COURSE OF AN AVERAGE DAY, somewhere in the world, a major medium-voltage electrical failure occurs at a facility. For many outages due to corrosion, heat build-up, insulation failures (some accelerated by contamination or humidity), animals, improperly prepared terminations, or misoperation, the cause is quickly identified and corrected, and the equipment is placed back in service. With properly designed, installed, and maintained protection systems, damage is usually limited in scope. However, in cases with extensive, and possibly collateral, damage, the cause may not be found until a thorough analysis and investigation is complete. Unfortunately, the conclusion is never appealing; often, the equipment or system was designed or installed incorrectly or did not perform as designed. Furthermore, the cause of many failures is either inconclusive or misdiagnosed. For those instances when the system did not perform as designed, there are two common causes: lack of maintenance and improper commissioning.

articleTitle: The year of continuing education
abstract: In the 1994 and 1999 IAS membership surveys, continuing education opportunities received the highest ranking when survey respondents were asked about future allocation of IAS resources. At the first IAS Congress, held in June 2001 in conjunction with the IEEE IAS Pulp and Paper Conference in Portland, Oregon, USA, one of the strategic issues discussed was the provision of more continuing education opportunities for our industrial members. Three action items related to continuing education opportunities were developed at the Congress: □ develop technology-focused, regional workshops □ develop asynchronous continuing education products □ restructure the IAS Education Department to focus on conference tutorials and asynchronous continuing education.

articleTitle: Society News
abstract: In the 1990s, the subject of International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) zone classifications was a frequent topic of discussion and technical papers at the PCIC, and the 1996 National Electrical Code (NEC) included zone classifications in Article 505. All of this was influenced by IEC standards for classified areas that were developed over the last two decades. One might ask, “Since the world seems to be converting to or adopting IEC standards, how do I, my company, or my technical society participate in the development and maintenance of these standards?” The answer is to be proactive and influence IEC standards through participation.

articleTitle: Recognizing outstanding IAS members
abstract: Plans continue for the 37th Annual Meeting and Technical Conference in Pittsburgh. Our title, Industry Applications Society, implies that support from industry is crucial to the success of the Society as well as the success of the Annual Meeting and Technical Conference. Pittsburgh is home to many of the industries that have been involved in our Society, and since the Local Committee is striving to make this the best IAS Technical Conference ever, we are calling on these industries for assistance. We have already honed in on three key corporate entities that have supported the IAS Annual Meeting for many years. Powerex, Robicon, and Bombardier will host our groups at their facilities during the technical tours. The Local Committee is arranging these tours so they do not conflict with the technical sessions related to the products manufactured at the tour sites. A metals facility may also be added to the industrial tour list.

articleTitle: An invitation to ias members from the ieee product safety committee
abstract: The technical committees in the IAS have a long history of involvement and influence in product safety leadership. Through the various Conferences and Standards Working Groups, manufacturers, users, and consultants have worked together to lead ongoing improvements in electrical equipment safety and performance. While many people have been involved in product safety, there has not been a specific focus on the discipline of product safety engineering within the IAS.

articleTitle: IAS Members lead change in "The other electrical hazard"
abstract: At the 1981 IAS Annual Meeting, held in Philadelphia, the Power System Protection Committee of the Industrial and Commercial Power Systems Department (I…CPSD) sponsored a landmark paper in the field of electrical safety. IAS Member and IEEE Fellow Ralph H. Lee presented his paper, “The Other Electrical Hazard: Electric Arc Blast Burns.” The arc hazard was not new; it had been present in industrial and commercial facilities since the beginning of electrification in the late 19th century. Historically, electric shock or electrocution hazards were viewed as the primary electrical hazards to workers. While the electric shock hazard is certainly important, it had masked a second important and unique electrical hazard associated with the intense radiant and convective energy released during an electric arc flash event. At the 1987 IAS Annual Meeting, in San Diego, the I…CPSD Power Systems Engineering Committee sponsored a panel discussion to further stimulate action to position arc flash hazards on par with electric shock. Over the two decades since Lee presented his paper, IAS members have led advancements in science and technology to better understand the arc flash phenomena and apply this knowledge in the evolution of technologies, regulations, standards, products and work practices to reduce the risk of injuries from the arc flash hazard.

articleTitle: Subject index
abstract: This index covers all technical items - papers, correspondence, reviews, etc. - that appeared in this periodical during the year, and items from previous years that were commented upon or corrected in this year. Departments and other items may also be covered if they have been judged to have archival value. The Author Index contains the primary entry for each item, listed under the first author's name. The primary entry includes the coauthors' names, the title of the paper or other item, and its location, specified by the publication abbreviation, year, month, and inclusive pagination. The Subject Index contains entries describing the item under all appropriate subject headings, plus the first author's name, the publication abbreviation, month, and year, and inclusive pages. Note that the item title is found only under he primary entry in the Author Index.

The IEEE Yellow Book
abstract: This column is devoted to a discussion of the IEEE Yellow Book. Officially, the Yellow Book is IEEE Standard 902, IEEE Guide for Maintenance, Operation, and Safety of Industrial and Commercial Power Systems. The IEEE Yellow Book is moving through the periodic revision process under the leadership of Michael Foley (m.foley@ieee.org). If you are interested in participating in the development of the IEEE Yellow Book, feel free to contact Chairperson Foley. Better yet, attend either the IAS Industrial and Commercial Power Systems conference (held each May) or the IAS Annual Meeting (held each October), get involved, and participate in person.
